subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: If √(1 − x²) + √(1 − y²) = a(x − y), show that dy/dx = √((1 − y²)/(1 − x²)).

mark_split.label: Substitute x = sin A and y = sin B
Apply the sum and difference formulas
Cancel and form cot((A − B)/2) = a
Read off that A − B is constant

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IB (2026-27 edition), book p.203, chapter 9 DIFFERENTIATION, Long Answer question 1. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the volume prints a CHAPTER-level marks banner (8M + 4M + 2 × 2M = 16M) but no per-step allocation on any answer. The split follows the shape this bank uses for a Maths-1B Section C question. This book prints almost no exam-appearance years, so appearances[] is empty — the chapter has long been examined, we simply have no sourced years for this question. Paper position: Maths-1B Section C runs Q19 to Q21 at 8 marks each, answer any 2 of 3, under the 2026-27 pattern. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The mathematics was checked independently before writing: for a = 2 and a = 5, matching pairs (x, y) were generated from Sin⁻¹x − Sin⁻¹y = 2 Cot⁻¹a, the original equation √(1 − x²) + √(1 − y²) = a(x − y) was confirmed to hold at each pair, and √((1 − y²)/(1 − x²)) matched a central difference quotient for dy/dx at every one — for example a = 2, x = 0.664852, y = −0.198669, both giving 1.312046639. The same check showed a domain limit worth knowing but outside what the question asks: for a fixed a, a value of x has a partner y only once Sin⁻¹x ≥ 2 Cot⁻¹a − π/2, so a small a admits only x close to 1. steps.why: Every term in the given equation is a square root of 1 minus a square, and 1 − sin²A = cos²A is the identity that removes exactly that. After the substitution no roots are left and the equation is an ordinary trigonometric one.
common_mistakes: Writing √(1 − sin²A) as ±cos A. The principal value of Sin⁻¹ keeps A in [−π/2, π/2], where cos A is not negative, so only the plus sign is possible.
Substituting x = tan A, which leaves √(1 − tan²A) and removes no root.
steps.memory_tip: A root of the form √(1 − x²) is usually removed by x = sin θ. Its partner √(1 + x²) is removed by x = tan θ.

common_mistakes: Writing sin C − sin D = 2 sin((C + D)/2) cos((C − D)/2), which puts the sine on the half sum. That is the formula for sin C + sin D.

steps.memory_tip: Cosine plus cosine keeps two cosines. Sine minus sine takes the cosine of the half sum and the sine of the half difference.
